title: REST API Design Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision of REST constraints, resource naming and nesting, filtering and sorting, request and response bodies, error formats, HATEOAS, and when to pick REST, GraphQL or gRPC.

chapters.title: REST Mental Model and Constraints
points: REST models everything as a resource (a noun) identified by a URI; clients exchange representations (usually JSON) of that resource's state
The six constraints: client-server, stateless, cacheable, uniform interface, layered system, code-on-demand (optional)
Stateless: every request carries all context (auth token, params); the server keeps no session between calls, which is what lets you scale horizontally
Methods: GET read (safe, idempotent), POST create (neither), PUT replace (idempotent), PATCH partial update (not guaranteed idempotent), DELETE remove (idempotent)
Interview Point: What makes an API RESTful rather than just HTTP? Why must REST be stateless? Which methods are safe and which are idempotent?

chapters.title: Resource Naming, Nesting and Status Codes
points: Name with plural nouns and lowercase kebab-case, never verbs: GET /orders/42, not /getOrder?id=42; the HTTP method is the verb
Nest only to show ownership, one or two levels deep: /users/7/orders is fine; /users/7/orders/42/items/3/reviews is not, so flatten to /items/3/reviews
Once an item has a globally unique ID, expose it at the top level (/orders/42) and keep the nested path (/users/7/orders) for listing
Non-CRUD actions: model them as a sub-resource or noun (POST /orders/42/cancellation), not as a verb in the path
Interview Point: When is nesting appropriate and when does it hurt? How do you model an action like 'cancel order' without a verb URL? What does POST return on create (201 plus Location header)?

chapters.title: Filtering, Sorting, Bodies and Error Formats
points: Filter, sort and paginate with query params on the collection: GET /orders?status=paid&sort=-created_at&limit=20&cursor=abc, where a '-' prefix means descending
Prefer cursor pagination over offset for large or changing data: offset slows down and skips or duplicates rows as data shifts
Bodies: send JSON with Content-Type: application/json; PUT needs the full object, PATCH sends only changed fields; return the created or updated resource in the response
Status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 bad input, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 422 validation failed, 429 rate limited, 500 server error
Error body should be consistent: { "type": "...", "title": "Validation failed", "status": 422, "detail": "email is invalid", "errors": [{ "field": "email" }] } (RFC 9457 problem+json shape)
Interview Point: Cursor vs offset pagination? 401 vs 403? What should a standard error response contain? PUT vs PATCH?

chapters.title: HATEOAS and REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC
points: HATEOAS: responses include links to the next valid actions, e.g. { "id": 42, "status": "pending", "_links": { "pay": "/orders/42/payment", "cancel": "/orders/42" } }, so clients follow links instead of hardcoding URLs; most real APIs skip it
REST: many resource endpoints over HTTP and JSON, easy HTTP caching, best for public APIs; the risks are over-fetching and under-fetching

GraphQL: one endpoint, and the client states exactly which fields it wants; it fixes over-fetching and suits varied clients like mobile, but HTTP caching is harder and costly queries need depth or complexity limits
gRPC: Protobuf over HTTP/2 with a strict contract, streaming and small payloads; best for internal service-to-service calls, but browsers need gRPC-Web and it is hard to debug by eye
Interview Point: What problem does HATEOAS solve? When would you pick GraphQL over REST, or gRPC over REST? Why is caching harder in GraphQL?

chapters.title: Common REST Design Mistakes
points: Verbs in URLs (/createUser, /deleteOrder) instead of nouns plus HTTP methods
Returning 200 with an error in the body, or using 500 for client mistakes, which breaks clients and monitoring
Using GET for actions that change state, which breaks the safe-method contract and lets crawlers or prefetchers trigger side effects
No versioning or pagination from the start: add /v1 (or a version header) and a limit on every collection, because unbounded lists break later
Interview Point: How would you version a public API? What goes wrong if a list endpoint has no pagination? Why should errors never come back as 200?

chapters.title: REST API Cheat Sheet
points: Methods: GET read, POST create, PUT replace, PATCH partial, DELETE remove; GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent
URLs: plural nouns, kebab-case, nest at most two levels, with query params for filter, sort and paginate (?status=paid&sort=-created_at&limit=20&cursor=...)
Pick: REST for public CRUD APIs, GraphQL for flexible client-driven queries, gRPC for fast internal service calls; HATEOAS is optional
Interview Point: Walk through designing GET, POST and error responses for an /orders API, and justify REST, GraphQL or gRPC for it.
